The strategy addresses security by applying AI in public safety, strengthening cybersecurity and data protection, enforcing ethical and legal standards for transparent use, and mitigating threats that could undermine peace and stability. It is also underlines the importance of international cooperation to prevent the unchecked or asymmetric use of AI technologies. We believe this approach is fully aligned with the objectives of the United Nations to safeguard peace, stability, and sustainable development in digital era. Distinguished members of Security Council, we see artificial intelligence as both a national priority for Uzbekistan and regional opportunity for Central Asia. Our region faces shared challenges, water scarcity, climate change, modernization of healthcare education, and development of cross regional transport corridors. AI can provide innovative solutions in areas such as water and agriculture, energy and healthcare, and connectivity. Central Asia has already demonstrated unity in addressing common challenges. A milestone came in July 2025 when U.N. General Assembly, at the initiative of Tajikistan, adopted a resolution of the role of AI in sustaining peace and development. Uzbekistan fully supported this initiative, reaffirming our commitment to advancing regional cooperation in AI and digitalization. We believe that through such steps, Central Asia can serve as a bridge between Asia and Europe in shaping a fair and inclusive digital future. At the global level, Uzbekistan attaches high importance to strengthening multilateral governance of AI. We have supported all four AI-related resolutions adopted by General Assembly in 2025, including those initiated by United States, China, Tajikistan, and resolution establishing a UN scientific panel and global dialogue on AI governance. Together, these documents represent a solid normative foundation. It is now vital for the Security Council to complement this work by focusing specifically on the peace and security dimensions of artificial intelligence. In this regard, the President of Uzbekistan, during the general debate of 80 session of General Assembly, proposed the creation of international cooperation mechanism for sharing applied AI solutions in healthcare, education and industry. This initiative aims to ensure that the results of scientific research and technological innovation accessible to all, especially to developing countries most in need. We hope for your support and cooperation in advancing this initiative. Mr. President, the world is changing with unprecedented speed. Artificial intelligence can become a driver of shared prosperity and sustainable peace, or catalyst of instability and insecurity. We must prevent digital inequality and technological divides. If left unaddressed, these gaps risk creating new dependencies, deepening instability and eroding trust among nations. Uzbekistan firmly believes that through dialogue, international cooperation, and full respect for the Charter of the United Nations, we can ensure that AI serves the purposes of peace, development, and human being. We stand ready to work with all member states to help shape a fair, safe, and inclusive digital future. Thank you.
I thank His Excellency Mr. Madraimov for the statement. I now give the floor to Ms. Cordula Dregge, Chief Legal Officer and Head of the Legal Division of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Mr. President, Excellencies, my remarks today are based on the ICRC's 160 years experience on the battlefield, where for every weapon introduced, our delegates have witnessed the results firsthand, not the results claimed by the developers and users, the good, the bad, and the unconscionable. We have identified three applications of AI in the military domain that pose significant risks: AI in autonomous weapon systems, in military decision-making, and in information and communication technologies. Promoters of these new AI applications underscore their military utility, but each of them also carries risks. AI-enabled autonomous weapons can engage their targets in communications denied environments, but AI increases the risk that human users will be unable to understand, predict, and control the weapon's effects, making it indiscriminate and unlawful under international humanitarian law. AI decision support systems can analyze vast amounts of data in seconds to produce recommendations for the commander. but their speed and scale, exacerbated by automation bias, might lead to simple rubber stamping, replacing human judgment rather than supporting it. AI-enabled cyber capabilities can identify and exploit new vulnerabilities in an enemy's computer systems. However, this also increases the risk of indiscriminate attacks, incidental damage to civilian infrastructure, and uncontrolled escalation of conflict. Mr. President, the claim that new weapons will be more humane, less lethal, more precise has been made by all promoters of new technologies on battlefields for as long as the ICRC can remember. Chemical weapons were advertised as more benign than artillery in the First World War, blinding laser weapons as less lethal than bullets in the 1980s, but this is not what we have seen historically and it is not what we are seeing now. If we contemplate today's most technologically sophisticated conflicts, we have not seen better outcomes for civilians, but rather the most appalling and indiscriminate devastation. The qualities advertised in new technologies have led not to precision, distinction and precaution, but to acceleration, amplification and escalation of destruction. The lesson is clear we must not allow these systems to continue to be developed without oversight and regulation, based on a realistic assessment of their compliance with international humanitarian law. I will close with two requests. First, to conclude as soon as possible a treaty on autonomous weapons systems, and second, to adopt a human-centered approach to military AI to ensure that human control and judgment are preserved in all decisions that pose risks to the life and dignity of people affected by war. Thank you very much.
